items.title: Normative boundaries of AI in scientific work: Evidence from PhD researchers
items.desc: Latent class analysis of 3,785 PhD students in STEM and health sciences (Nature Graduate Survey 2025) identifies four distinct attitudinal profiles toward AI use in research. The dominant profile reflects a 'division of labour' in which AI is broadly accepted for literature tracking and summarising but far less so for core tasks like designing experiments and analysing data. [arXiv econ.GN, posted 2026-08-26]

items.title: The Reverse Big Push: Generative AI and Self-Fulfilling Automation
items.desc: Models a local service economy where generative AI shifts the fixed cost of automation from the firm to a model provider, so the firm rents capability by usage instead of carrying payroll. Because payroll itself supports demand, production modes can become strategic complements and the economy can support both a high-demand human-augmented equilibrium and a low-demand automated one, with the former the local first best. [arXiv econ.TH, posted 2026-08-26]

items.title: Nvidia's Profit Doubles to $59.69 Billion Thanks to A.I. Spending
items.desc: Nvidia reported that quarterly profit doubled to $59.69 billion, driven by continued heavy capital spending on AI infrastructure by its largest customers. [NYT Technology, published 2026-08-26]

items.title: Wall St. Scrutinizes Nvidia's Deal Machine
items.desc: DealBook examines investor unease about Nvidia's web of investments in the AI companies that also buy its chips, and what that circularity means for how the earnings should be read. [NYT DealBook, published 2026-08-26]

items.title: This Is How the A.I. Debt Binge Sinks the Economy
items.desc: An opinion piece arguing that debt-financed AI data-centre buildouts by hyperscalers carry macroeconomic risk, tracing how the borrowing could propagate into the broader economy if returns disappoint. [NYT Opinion, published 2026-08-26]

items.title: Meta Took Aim at Anthropic. It Is Also One of Its Largest Customers.
items.desc: Reports on the commercially entangled relationship between Meta and Anthropic, where the two compete publicly while Meta remains a major buyer of Anthropic's models — an illustration of how AI supply relationships blur rivalry and dependence. [NYT Technology, published 2026-08-27]
